title: Imaging the topological sign of a Dirac mass with spin-polarized tunneling
authors: Payman Kazemikhah, Ruolun Zhang, Byunghoon Kim, Xiangyu Luo, Zachary Ducorsky, Yu-Peng Zhu, Md. Shafayat Hossain, M. Zahid Hasan
abstract: A Dirac mass is characterized not only by its magnitude but also by its sign, which influences the Berry curvature, Hall response, and the propagation direction of chiral boundary modes. However, local spectroscopy of magnetic topological surfaces has so far accessed only the gap magnitude $|M|$. Here we show how the topological sign of $M$ can be determined locally. We first establish the sign information that spin-resolved tunneling can access and the reference required to obtain an absolute Hall sign. Although spin--orbital entanglement generally obscures the relation between measured spin and Dirac pseudospin, crystalline rotation symmetry alleviates this ambiguity at the band edge. On a $C_3$ axis, an axial tip couples to a fully spin-polarized state whose tunneling asymmetry directly reveals the sign of the occupied-band Berry curvature, independent of orbital composition. We further show that the zeroth Landau level provides an independent mass-sign measurement with an unpolarized tip, while opposite domains and their chiral domain-wall modes provide self-consistency checks. These results pave the way for imaging the locations where the topological character changes within a material, rather than merely identifying where a spectral gap appears.
summary: This paper presents a novel method to locally determine the sign of the Dirac mass in magnetic topological materials using spin-polarized scanning tunneling microscopy. By exploiting crystalline rotation symmetry, the technique allows researchers to map the sign of the Berry curvature in real space, moving beyond merely identifying where a spectral gap exists. This capability is crucial for understanding the full topological character of materials.
main_problem: The primary goal is to develop a local spectroscopic technique capable of determining the topological sign of a Dirac mass ($M$), which is crucial because current methods only measure the gap magnitude $|M|$.
main_result: The authors demonstrate that spin-resolved tunneling, particularly when exploiting crystalline rotation symmetry on a $C_3$ axis, can directly and locally measure the sign of the occupied-band Berry curvature, $	ext{sgn}(\Omega_{	ext{occ}})$.
method: The method combines theoretical modeling of magnetic topological surfaces with proposed experimental measurements using spin-polarized scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) spectroscopy.
model_or_system: The study models magnetic topological surfaces exhibiting a Dirac cone gapped by an exchange mass $M$. The analysis uses tight-binding models, continuum Hamiltonians, and incorporates effects from spin-polarized tunneling tips and domain wall structures.
key_observables: Spin asymmetry $A(E)$, the sign of the Berry curvature ($	ext{sgn}(\Omega_{	ext{occ}})$), and the energy/spin characteristics of chiral domain-wall modes.
important_parameters: The mass $M$, the tip polarization $P$, the crystalline symmetry axis ($C_3$), and the disorder strength ($\delta M$).
main_assumptions: The technique relies on the existence of crystalline rotation symmetry ($C_n$ axis) to simplify the spin-orbital entanglement and ensure the band-edge state is fully spin-polarized.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the readout mechanism using spin-polarized tips on $C_3$ axes, showing spin reversal with $M$, and confirming the relationship between measured spin asymmetry and the Berry curvature sign. Other figures detail domain wall physics and the robustness of the sign measurement against disorder.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the physical necessity of measuring the mass sign to detailing the symmetry-protected measurement protocol using spin-polarized STM, and finally validating the technique by analyzing domain walls and disordered systems.
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete, measurable spectroscopic signature ($	ext{sgn}(\Omega_{	ext{occ}})$) that goes beyond simple gap measurements, offering a powerful tool for mapping topological phase transitions in real space, which is highly relevant for understanding topological materials in condensed matter physics.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Local readout of the Dirac-mass sign. (a) A spin-polarized tip with reversible polarization ±Pz probes a C3 axis of a magnetic topological-insulator surface. Domains with opposite exchange masses M have opposite Berry curvatures, and their boundary hosts a chiral mode with in-plane spin perpendicular to the wall. (b) Massive Dirac spectra for the two domains, colored by ⟨σz⟩. The band-edge spin reverses with M; the dashed line marks the zeroth Landau level, E0 = −M for eB > 0. (c) Rotation-axis selection rule. For the band-edge state αpz↑+βp+↓, the m = 1 component vanishes on the C3 axis, so an axial tip couples to a fully polarized state, ceff z = 1, independent of the orbital...

FIG. 2. On-axis spin equals the Hall sign. Selection rule in a C3v spin–orbital model (p orbitals, spin–orbit and orbital Rashba coupling, exchange along z, SM S6). (a) Deviation 1 −|ceff z | of the tip polarization of the upper band edge along the cell diagonal for three tip heights. It vanishes on the C3 axes. The zero at the bridge site reflects the model’s twofold axis. (b) Tip asymmetry near the gap on and off the axis, and orbital-traced. Dashed, Eq. (5) with δ = −0.23. The orbital-traced polarization has the opposite sign at both edges (+0.16, −0.48). (c) For 250 random parameter sets, the on-axis spin of the upper edge always equals sgn Ωocc. The orbital-traced spin has either sign.

FIG. 3. Domain walls as self-calibrating controls. Domain walls in the doubler-free continuum model (M0 = 0.3, wall width 0.9 v/M0, η = 0.1M0). (a) log10 ρ0 with the in-gap Jackiw–Rebbi mode. (b) ρz/ρ0, exactly antisymmetric about the wall. (c) At E = 0 the mode has spin perpendicular to the wall (ρx/ρ0 = −0.82) and is invisible to a z tip. (d) Cuts at E = 1.2M0 for the continuum (±0.73) and lattice F1 (+0.57, −0.77). The asymmetry of F1 comes from its time-reversal-odd regulator.

FIG. 4. Field route, decision statistics, and tip-induced mass. (a) Landau levels for eB > 0 (lower) and eB < 0 (upper) for the continuum with curvature (solid) and lattice F1 (dotted), M = 0.3, 2πϕ = 0.031, with E0 = −sgn(eB)(M −β|eB|). (b) Probability of a correct decision at 99% confidence, Eq. (7) (lines) and Monte Carlo (circles), M = 15 meV. (c) Bias from a tip-induced mass in fits that use one side of the gap, 1/E only versus joint fit. The band marks ±1 standard error at σ = 0.01G0.
